paras: Every review is positive, and most describe a balanced, power-leaning hybrid, with two placing it just below the Selkirk Boomstick for power. Reviewers disagree on control: one found the pop hard to control until weight was added, while another calls it the most forgiving paddle in a four-way comparison, though with less spin than grittier options. Testing ran from a few days to about two months.

Reviewers describe a mid-to-high power hybrid that suits intermediate and advanced players, most often measured against the 11SIX24 Power 2 or its elongated sibling, the J6CR. They disagree on control: some call it easy to keep in play, while one mixed take finds the pop tricky to control, needing a week or two and added weight to settle. Another mixed take dislikes the short handle and throat taper, and one reviewer's first unit arrived with weak grit, a problem another says others have reported.

Many reviewers treat it as an upgrade on the original Coral, with a little more power and spin but a crisper, firmer feel, and several note it is UPA approved only. It suits all-court and control-first players, roughly 3.0 to 4.5 by one reviewer. Two of the three mixed takes say it is too low on power and unstable off-center for singles or top-level play (Rackets & Runners), or plays as a power paddle with little dwell that lower-level players may not enjoy (SupaSenpai).

Most note it runs heavy for a hybrid, and reviewers mostly compare it with the Bread & Butter Loco, with several saying it pops less. The one mixed review, from Pickleball3en, found volley rolls at the kitchen popped too much, so pop is where they disagree. The five who checked found little grit wear.

No review is negative, and many pitch the paddle at beginners, newer players and anyone who struggles with control, often as a strong value under $100. The usual caveat is that power and pop are modest, and several say it cannot match thermoformed paddles. Reviewers split on the thin 14mm version, with two rejecting it and two praising it, and the Hyperion is the most common comparison.

Nikki Maldonado calls it the ultimate soft game paddle for doubles but not a singles paddle, and says drives need extra effort. Pickleball Studio, The Pickleball Dad, Pickleball Effect and Johnkew Pickleball each say it is not for players who want maximum power or aggression. Johnkew, Matt's Pickleball and Pickleball Effect all rate the Power 2 Pegasus ahead of it on power.

Drill More Pickleball, the one negative take, found the wide body too poppy at the kitchen, rates it B tier and prefers the Ultre. Pickleball Tech Dude, one of the three mixed takes, reports the area above the corners is a dead zone. Pickle Bill recommends it for doubles and Matthew K Pickleball for control lovers, while Pickleball Adventure warns of pop ups when touch is off.

highlights.text: pop ups when touch is off

paras: Four takes are mixed. West Side Pickleball picks the Loco 2 by a narrow edge, and PBVinny's TikTok prefers the J2CR feel. Pickleball On Call rated control 3.5 out of 10 and found the sweet spot hit or miss, and Matt's Pickleball says sloppy shots float and suggests it for bangers.

Eight reviewers flag that it is not USAP approved. Of the three mixed takes, Famous by Friday Pickleball saw occasional flyers, Pickle Li needed added weight for good spin and called it possibly overhyped for spin, and Paddle Review Hub found the feel good but not exceptional. Pickleheads says it suits 3.5 and up players who use spin or added weight.

Salt N Pepper Pickleball, one of the two mixed takes, popped balls up at the kitchen and steers beginners and inconsistent players toward the J2 line. The other, Ignatowich HQ, found power one step below the Loco and resets never fully comfortable. Pickleheads rates it for players around 4.0 to 4.5, and Pickleball Playbook for 4.25 and above.

highlights.text: popped balls up at the kitchen

paras: Three takes are mixed. Pickleball Willy worries a honeycomb core at $280 will lose its life quickly, Pickleball Studio calls the update minor and warns it is a poor fit when popups and soft game problems exist, and Matt's Pickleball's TikTok finds it firmer with less spin than the RPM Friction Pro. Pickleball Studio, Pickleball Effect and Johnkew Pickleball all point to the cheaper 11SIX24 Power series.

Reviewers disagree on where it sits. Womack Pickleball and Pickleball Pursuit call it all court, Pickleball Medicine rates the series best for control, and JJ Pickleball classes it as a lower end power paddle. Six reviewers call the E shape niche, narrow or unstable, and five mention a break-in that changes the feel, with Johnkew telling control players to wait.

Several reviewers limit it to advanced or aggressive players: Ignatowich HQ, Matt's Pickleball, Pickleball Effect and West Side Pickleball, which sets 4.0 to 4.5 as the minimum. The two negative takes, a West Side video and a Pickleball Paddle Reviews TikTok, call it high risk or very hard to control, and the TikTok calls the newer Boulder Opal an upgrade with a bigger sweet spot.

Smash Pickleball and Pickleball_Ace, two of the three mixed takes, both rate its power below the Loco, and Smash found it too soft to calibrate dinks. West Side Pickleball, the third, felt off on drops. Pickleheads and The Kitchen Pickleball point power seekers to the Black Opal, and Matt's Pickleball says banger style players will not enjoy it.

Despite the control label, Pickleball Studio calls it a power paddle, and Pickleball Effect finds more pop than a typical raw carbon paddle. Pickleball Studio would not recommend it to players who struggle with resets. The one mixed take, from Pickleball Effect, did not take to it right away and added lead tape for a plusher feel, comparing it with the Carbon X series. Mid-Century Pickleball argues all court paddles suit players moving up levels.

Womack Pickleball, the one negative review, found a small sweet spot with a significant drop in pop and power off center and calls it hard to recommend at $200. Of the three mixed takes, Pickleball Tech Dude says it needs a lot of weight modification, West Side Pickleball calls the sweet spot small and limited to the center, and The Pickleball Pirates notes power drops on off-center hits. Famous by Friday says it is begging for weight.

Pickleball Pursuit, one of the two mixed takes, saw the grit lose spin after about 3 to 4 hours and prefers the J2K. The other, Pickleball Effect, still controls the Double Black Diamond better and needed a few sessions to adjust to the pop. Pickleball Studio and Dash Pickleball say Double Black Diamond owners need not upgrade.

highlights.text: controls the Double Black Diamond better

paras: Matthew K Pickleball calls it a strong choice for control lovers, but Pickleball Medicine, Pickleball Pursuit, STS Pickleball and All Drive No Drop Pickleball place it in the all court category. Six reviewers compare its play with the Volair Mach 2 Forza, and five of them find the Forza more controllable. Pickleball Studio finds the stock paddle vibrates and says it needs lead tape to reach its potential.

Four takes are mixed. UnforcedErrorsPB, in both a review and a TikTok, found the Flash head heavy and sluggish at the kitchen, Pickle Techie found it slow there with little pop, and Pickleheads rated control below the Prism Flash. Six reviewers frame it as an upgrade for Prism players.

Dwell Time Pickleball recommends it for players 4.0 and below, and Pickleheads for 3.0 to 4.5, though Pickleheads warns beginners may find the feedback off-putting. The one mixed take, from Matt's Pickleball, found it inconsistent out of the box and recommends it only for players willing to tinker. Four reviewers compare it with the Quanta, and Pickleball Studio finds the Pro more playable out of the box.

highlights.text: more playable out of the box
